The Data Science Center helps UCLA researchers and humanists get more out
of their data and their work: one-on-one consultations, hands-on training,
and the shared infrastructure that keeps that work usable for years after
it's published.

## Four findings (2017-2026, periods noted)

1. Reach spans nearly every part of campus, not one department. Of 1,575
   UCLA-affiliated workshop-attendance records, 838 map to a known school,
   division, or institute. The rest are recorded but lack department
   information; they aren't concentrated in one unresolved corner of
   campus (2017-2024, `claim-register.md` #6).

2. Direct, one-on-one support is substantial on its own. DSC has
   recorded about 1,850 research consultations since 2017, rising to
   341-394 a year in 2021-2023. Recording lapsed from mid-2024, when the
   scheduling system changed during staff turnover, so later years are
   floors; the work continued. These are interactions, not unique people
   (`claim-register.md` #10).

3. Training builds capacity that outlasts the workshop. Since 2017 DSC
   has run 819 workshop sessions with about 18,700 attendee-events,
   including the UC-wide Carpentries series it co-founded and co-delivers
   (`claim-register.md` #8-9). At least 39
   people who came through DSC-supported UC Carpentries workshops
   (2021-2025) have since been publicly confirmed in research or
   data-intensive roles. Call this an early signal, not a tracer study:
   role start dates weren't verified, so it shows association, not that
   DSC caused the outcome (`claim-register.md` #3-5).

4. Shared infrastructure is doing real, cited work. UCLA Dataverse, which
   DSC operates, holds 377 published datasets and 25,330 files, with
   143,414 recorded downloads. At least 13 linked publications have drawn
   258 citations so far (`infrastructure.qmd`, live KPI).

## One case

Carceral Ecologies, a project of UCLA's Institute for Society and
Genetics, needed to process a helicopter-surveillance dataset. DSC and
DataSquad provided years of support: R server infrastructure, data
processing, and hands-on training for a research student who's still
using those skills. One processing task that used to take about 318
minutes now takes about 2, roughly a 159-fold speedup, and the underlying
research has drawn coverage from the Los Angeles Times, The New Yorker,
and Bloomberg (`claim-register.md` #1).

## The ask

Keep this capacity intact while the Library's structure changes. That
means a commitment that DSC's consultation, instruction, and
infrastructure services continue at their current scope, with the
staffing and budget authority to run them, until the new structure is
settled. The 2024-2025 recording gap shows what a lapse costs: the work
went on, but the record of it didn't.

## Evidence, periods, and units

| Finding | Source | Period | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Department/division reach | Org-parent crosswalk (tested) | 2017-2024 | Attendee-event record |
| Consultations (about 1,850) | Calendly, LibInsight, LibCal series | 2017-2026 | Consultation record |
| Workshops (819 / about 18,700) | Reconciled attendance, incl. UC-wide Carpentries | 2017-2026 | Session / attendee-event |
| Trajectory signal (39) | Named-people identity passes, deduped | 2021-2025 attendance | Person, public confirmation |
| Dataverse metrics | Dataverse API + OpenAlex | Cumulative to date | Dataset / file / download / citation |
| Case study | Impact case-study log | Multi-year engagement | Documented engagement |

: Full paths and methods for each row are in `claim-register.md`.

## Limitations

- The reach finding uses the attendee-level records for 2017-2024
  (15,765). 5,722 of those have unknown UCLA affiliation and are excluded
  from it, not treated as non-UCLA. The since-2017 workshop total adds
  the UC-wide Carpentries series and 2024-2026 sessions; about 235 of
  those later attendee-events haven't had the full duplication check.
- The trajectory finding isn't a tracer study. No pass captured a role
  start date, so a confirmed later role doesn't establish that it began
  after DSC engagement, and coverage hasn't been systematically
  re-verified.
- Consultations are a floor from mid-2024 on. Calendly ended in mid-2024
  and LibCal wasn't in use until May 2025, across two reorganizations.
  LibCal shows consultations continued through the gap, so the drop in
  recorded consultations is a recording gap, not a measured decline in
  demand. The series counts interactions, not unique people.
- One case study is illustrative, not representative, of DSC's full
  range of work. A broader set covering instruction and infrastructure
  engagements specifically is in progress.
